sections.h2: Is Queens a county or a borough, and why does that matter for tax?
sections.html:
Queens is both. Since 1899 the borough has been coextensive with Queens County, so the county has no separate government and property tax in Queens is billed by the New York City Department of Finance. Finance also values every parcel in the borough.

Queens County dates to 1683 and was named for Catherine of Braganza. Until 1899 it also included what is now Nassau County. The 1898 consolidation of New York City folded in the towns of Long Island City, Newtown, Flushing and Jamaica. The borough covers 178 square miles, 109 of them land, and is home to both LaGuardia and John F. Kennedy airports, Flushing Meadows-Corona Park and Citi Field.

Mail zones still follow the old towns: ZIP codes beginning 111 serve Long Island City, 113 Flushing, 114 Jamaica and 116 Far Rockaway. The Department of Finance identifies a parcel by borough, block and lot.

sections.h2: When are Queens property tax bills due?
sections.html:
The city's tax year runs from July 1 to June 30. Finance mails bills four times a year, and the number of payments you make depends on assessed value. A property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed quarterly, with due dates on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. Above $250,000, bills come twice a year, due July 1 and January 1.

Quarterly payers have a grace period through the 15th of the due month. Because the next date is January 1, 2027, a payment postmarked by January 15 is interest-free for a quarterly property. A weekend or holiday moves a due date to the next business day.

Paying the rest of the year early earns a discount of 0.50 percent in July, 0.33 percent in October and 0.17 percent in January, according to the Department of Finance. If you prepaid part of the year, ask your attorney whether that payment is credited at closing.

sections.h2: How much interest does a Queens late payment cost?
sections.html:
Interest on late tax compounds daily and is set each fiscal year by local law according to assessed value. For July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 the rates are 6 percent for assessed value up to $250,000, 9 percent above $250,000 up to $450,000 and 16 percent above $450,000.

  • Assessed value up to $250,000: 6 percent a year.
  • Over $250,000 up to $450,000: 9 percent.
  • Over $450,000: 16 percent.

The city says an owner is responsible for paying on time even when no bill arrives, so confirm that Finance has your current mailing address. For tax class 2 properties with more than ten units and all class 4 properties, interest is based on the actual assessed value before phase-in. Finance also runs payment agreements and a program called PT AID, which lets eligible homeowners defer tax or pay a percentage based on income.

sections.h2: What is the Queens tax lien sale?
sections.html:
New York City sells liens on unpaid property tax to a single authorized buyer. This is not a sale of the house, but the buyer can start foreclosure within one year after the sale date if the lien is not paid or put under a payment agreement. The most recent sale on the Finance page was held on June 3, 2025.

After a sale you owe the tax plus a 5 percent surcharge, daily compounding interest at 6, 9 or 16 percent by assessed value, and administrative costs that include an estimated $300 for notices. The city notifies owners by mail within 90 days of the sale, and the owner then deals with the new lienholder named in the letter, not with anyone who calls unprompted.

  • One-family owner-occupied homes become eligible with $5,000 or more of property tax debt that is three years overdue.
  • Two to three family homes have the same property tax test, plus a $3,000 water and sewer test at one year.
  • Residential condos and co-ops use $5,000 and three years for property tax.
  • Active duty military personnel may ask to be excluded.

Owners whose primary residence is the Queens property, who own no other New York City property, and whose combined annual income is no more than $110,750 may apply to waive the 5 percent surcharge.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Queens assessment?
sections.html:
Finance sends a Notice of Property Value around January 15 each year. It carries the estimated market value, the tentative assessed value, the tax class and any exemptions. If the property facts are wrong, Finance corrects them. If you dispute the assessed value, tax class or an exemption, the independent Tax Commission handles that review.

You must file an Application for Correction, and the Tax Commission has to receive it by the deadline, which cannot be extended: March 1 for tax class 2, 3 and 4, and March 15 for class 1. Class 1 valuation claims use Form TC108. You can file in person or by mail at One Centre Street, Room 2400 in Manhattan, or at the Queens Business Center of the Department of Finance, 144-06 94th Avenue, first floor. The commission's home page says this year filing by email is not allowed.

The 2026 tax rate for class 1 is 19.843 percent, for class 2 it is 12.439 percent, for class 3 it is 11.108 percent and for class 4 it is 10.848 percent. Exemptions such as STAR, senior citizen, veteran and disability can be reviewed on separate forms with a May 31 deadline.

sections.h2: How do I sell a Queens house when tax is overdue?
sections.html:
Ask the Department of Finance for the amount you owe and whether your parcel was included in a lien sale. Call 311 if the bill is unclear. If a lien was sold, the payoff goes to the new lienholder named in the city's letter, while current charges still go to the city.

  1. Pull a statement for the borough, block and lot and match it to your closing date.
  2. Learn whether any water or sewer debt sits on the same account.
  3. Close your STAR registration if you have one, and keep any assessment appeal papers for your attorney.
  4. Pay all debts from the sale proceeds at the closing table through your attorney.

A cash buyer will take a Queens house with arrears, repairs and tenants, and can close faster than a financed buyer who needs an appraisal. Ask for the offer in writing before you set a date.

faqs.q: Who bills property tax in Queens County?
faqs.a: The New York City Department of Finance bills it. Queens has been coextensive with the county since 1899, so there is no county treasurer or town collector. The Queens Business Center is at 144-06 94th Avenue, first floor, and 311 handles questions.

faqs.q: When is the next Queens property tax payment due?
faqs.a: The next due date is January 1, 2027 for quarterly and semi-annual payers. Quarterly payers get a grace period through January 15. If the due date falls on a weekend or federal holiday, payment is due the next business day.

faqs.q: What interest rate applies to late Queens property tax?
faqs.a: The rate is 6 percent for assessed value up to $250,000, 9 percent from there to $450,000 and 16 percent above $450,000, from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. Interest compounds daily, so late payments cost more each day.

faqs.q: Can the city sell my house over unpaid tax in Queens?
faqs.a: The city sells the debt, not the house, in a lien sale to an authorized buyer. That lienholder can begin foreclosure within one year after the sale if the debt is unpaid and no payment agreement exists. One-family owner-occupied homes qualify for sale with $5,000 of tax debt three years overdue.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Queens assessed value?
faqs.a: File an Application for Correction with the Tax Commission. It must be received by March 1 for tax classes 2, 3 and 4, or March 15 for class 1, and filing is in person or by mail. Use Form TC108 for a class 1 valuation claim.
